title: A surah sent down so you would remember.
subtitle: Why An-Nur opens by naming its own weight

key.label: What kind of text this is

row.title: a trust
sub: given to be lived and remembered

then: Ibn Kathir notes that Allah opens this surah by pointing to its high standing. Mujahid and Qatadah said it lays out {idea}what is lawful and unlawful, commands and limits.{/idea} It came in Madinah, as the young community faced questions about family, honor, and trust.
now: You save a long post called "rules for a healthy home" and never open it again. Most of us treat guidance like that: good to have, easy to forget. This surah says up front that it is {idea}not a bookmark.{/idea} It was sent so you would remember it when life gets messy.
old: Guidance is something I read once and agree with.
new: Guidance is something Allah sent down to stay in my memory and my home.
try: Before reading the rest of this surah, ask Allah to help you remember one thing from it this week.

title: Allah treats the sanctity of intimacy as no small thing.
subtitle: A serious limit, set in public, for a serious harm

row.title: a set limit
sub: for a court, not a mob

row.title: a limit of Allah
sub: tied to belief in the Last Day

then: The verse treats this wrong as weighty, a limit of Allah and not a private matter. Ibn Kathir explains that the forbidden pity is the kind that would make a judge drop Allah's limit, {idea}not the natural softness of a heart.{/idea} A Companion who felt pity even when slaughtering a sheep was told he would be {reward}rewarded for that feeling.{/reward}
now: Late at night, a chat that started as harmless keeps getting warmer. A voice says nobody gets hurt, it is just between two people. The verse answers that voice from far away: {trap}Allah does not see this as small.{/trap} The seriousness is there to make you stop long before any line.
old: What happens between two consenting adults is nobody else's business.
new: Allah counts this as a weighty trust, and the weight is meant to protect me early.
try: Notice one door that tends to lead you toward what you would regret. Close it gently today.

title: Who you bind your life to says who you are becoming.
subtitle: Like is drawn to like in the choice of a spouse

row.title: an open sinner
sub: who sees no wrong in it

row.title: the same
sub: or one who denies it is wrong

then: Ibn Kathir reports that a believer asked the Prophet ﷺ about marrying a woman known for selling herself, who had offered to support him. The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse in reply. Qatadah and Muqatil said it {idea}kept believers from marrying into open immorality.{/idea}
now: Your friend is choosing someone mostly for the money, the looks, or the follower count. You know the values do not match, but nobody says it. This verse says it plainly: {idea}the person you choose shapes the home you will live in.{/idea}
old: Character can be fixed after the wedding.
new: The character I look for in a spouse shows the character I want for myself.
try: Write down the three qualities you would most want in a life partner. Ask if you are building them in yourself.

title: An accusation without proof stains the accuser.
subtitle: Why a chaste person's honor is guarded so strongly

row.title: he must prove it
sub: or he is the one exposed

then: This verse set a very high bar for anyone accusing a chaste person. Ibn Kathir explains that an accuser without proof is himself held to account, and {trap}his word loses its trust{/trap} before Allah and people. The same holds if the one accused is a man.
now: Someone in the office group chat drops a hint about a colleague's private life. No proof, just "people are saying." The verse flips the room: {idea}the person who speaks without proof is the one on trial.{/idea} Their word loses its value.
old: If I only repeat what I heard, I am not responsible.
new: A claim about someone's honor makes me answerable for every word of it.
try: The next time a rumor reaches you, ask: do I actually know this? If not, let it stop with you.

title: Even the slanderer is offered a way back.
subtitle: Repentance and repair reopen the door
then: Right after the warning, Allah makes an exception for those who repent and reform. Ibn Kathir notes that many early scholars, including Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib, held that a repentant accuser {reward}is no longer called rebellious.{/reward} Some added that he must {idea}admit he spoke falsely.{/idea}
now: Years ago you said something about someone that was not true. It spread. You think about it at red lights. The verse does not leave you stuck there. {reward}Turn back, and fix what you can,{/reward} even if it is one honest message saying you were wrong.
old: What I said is out there now. Nothing I do changes it.
new: Allah is Forgiving, and repair is part of turning back.
try: If you once spread something untrue about someone, take one small step to correct it today.

title: When a husband has no witness but himself.
subtitle: A way out given to a man in an impossible spot

key.label: What Allah did with the impasse

then: After the verse on accusers, Sa'd bin Ubadah asked how a man could fetch four witnesses in such a moment. Soon Hilal bin Umayyah came home and found a man with his wife. The Prophet ﷺ was troubled, and Hilal said he hoped {idea}Allah would make a way out.{/idea} Then this verse came, and the Prophet ﷺ told him, {reward}Rejoice, O Hilal.{/reward}
now: You are in a situation where the truth is real to you but you cannot prove it to anyone. Saying it might cost you. Staying quiet is eating you. Hilal's story is for that corridor: {reward}Allah knows, and He makes ways out{/reward} that you cannot see yet.
old: If I cannot prove it, my truth counts for nothing.
new: Allah knows what I know, and He can open a way I never imagined.
try: Bring one situation where you feel unheard to Allah tonight, in your own words, like Hilal did.

title: The fifth oath puts his own soul on the line.
subtitle: Truth spoken with the curse of Allah as its price

row.title: the curse of Allah
sub: on me, if I am lying

row.title: a pledge before Allah
sub: with your own soul as surety

then: In Hilal's case, before the fifth oath he was told to have taqwa, because {trap}the punishment of this world is easier than that of the Hereafter.{/trap} He replied that Allah would not punish him for it, just as He had not let him be flogged. Then he swore the fifth.
now: "I swear to God" slips out in arguments, in sales calls, in teenage fights over who broke the charger. This verse shows what an oath is meant to be: {idea}you put yourself under Allah's judgment.{/idea} That is why the last oath pauses everyone in the room.
old: Swearing by Allah is just a way of saying I am serious.
new: Swearing by Allah places my own soul as the guarantee of my words.
try: Go one full day without casually swearing by Allah. Keep it for when it truly matters.

title: She is given her own voice, four times.
subtitle: The accused is not left defenseless
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the wife is given her own four oaths by Allah that her husband is lying. In the story, the Prophet ﷺ {idea}recited the verses to both of them{/idea} and reminded them that the Hereafter is weightier than this world.
now: In family disputes, the louder person often wins. The one with more relatives in the room. The one who tells the story first. This verse gives the accused {idea}an equal chance to speak before Allah,{/idea} and leaves the final knowledge with Him.
old: Whoever speaks first and loudest is probably right.
new: Allah gives both sides a voice, and He alone knows who is true.
try: In your next disagreement, let the other person finish their side before you answer.

title: The wrath named is for one who knows the truth.
subtitle: Why her fifth oath mentions Allah's anger

row.title: the wrath of Allah
sub: on me, if he is truthful

row.title: wrath
sub: for knowing truth and turning away

then: Ibn Kathir notes the wrath of Allah is named in her oath because {trap}wrath falls on one who knows the truth yet deviates from it.{/trap} In the story, at the fifth oath she hesitated and almost admitted, then said she would not shame her people, and swore.
now: You know you broke the thing. You know you sent the message. Someone asks, and the easy word is "no." This verse points at that moment: {idea}the gap between what you know and what you say{/idea} is where the real danger lives.
old: If no one can prove it, denying it costs me nothing.
new: Denying what I know to be true is the heaviest thing I could do.
try: Admit one small thing today that you would usually deny, even if it is just to yourself before Allah.

title: Without His mercy, life would be too hard to bear.
subtitle: The grace behind every way out

key.label: Where the way out came from

row.title: His grace
sub: or it would have crushed us

then: After laying out the oaths, Allah reminds the believers of His grace. Ibn Kathir explains that {reward}without it, many of their affairs would have been too difficult.{/reward} He accepts repentance from His servants, even after a sworn oath, and is Wise in what He commands.
now: Think back to the worst week of your marriage, your job, your family. Somehow there was a way through. A talk that happened at the right time. A door that opened. {reward}That was grace,{/reward} not luck, and it is still on offer.
old: I got through the hard times because I was strong.
new: I got through because Allah's grace made a way, and He still accepts me back.
try: Thank Allah for one specific way out He gave you in the past. Name it out loud.

title: The worst month of her life was written as good.
subtitle: The slander against Aishah, and the hidden good in it
then: Aishah went looking for a lost necklace and the army left without her. Safwan bin Al-Mu'attal found her and led his camel back to the army. {trap}Abdullah bin Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites, made up a lie{/trap} and whispered it until others repeated it. For almost a month she wept, until Allah {reward}revealed her innocence.{/reward}
now: Someone spread a story about you at work or in the family. You lie awake replaying it. People you trusted look at you differently. This verse speaks to that night: {reward}it is not only bad for you.{/reward} Allah sees it, and every person who spread it {trap}carries their own share.{/trap}
old: Being lied about can only ruin me.
new: Allah can turn even a lie told about me into good, and each liar carries their own load.
try: If you are carrying a hurt from gossip about you, tell Allah plainly tonight and leave the accounting to Him.

title: Why did you not think good of your own?
subtitle: The first reaction a believer owes a rumor
then: Ibn Kathir reports that Umm Ayyub asked her husband about the talk. Abu Ayyub said it was lies, and asked if she would ever do such a thing. She said no. {idea}He said Aishah was better than her.{/idea} The verse also notes she arrived {reward}openly at midday with the whole army watching.{/reward}
now: A message lands in the family group: "Did you hear about her?" Your thumb hovers. Before replying, do what Abu Ayyub did. {idea}Would I do that? Then why assume they did?{/idea} Thinking good happens in the heart. Saying "this is a lie" happens on your phone.
old: I am not judging, I am just asking if it is true.
new: A believer's first move is to think good of their own and say so.
try: Next time you hear something bad about someone, say one good thing you know about them instead.

title: No proof means the liar is the one speaking.
subtitle: How Allah names an unproven claim
then: The people of the slander spoke with confidence, but brought no proof. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah asked why they did not bring witnesses to prove what they said, and since they did not, {trap}with Allah they are the liars.{/trap}
now: Online, a post accuses someone. Thousands share it. No one checked. It feels true because so many people are saying it. This verse measures it a different way: {idea}no proof, no right to say it.{/idea} The crowd does not turn a rumor into a fact.
old: If enough people are saying it, there must be something to it.
new: Without proof, the claim condemns the one making it, not the one it is about.
try: Before you share or forward a claim about anyone today, ask what proof you actually have.

title: Mercy is the only reason they were not ruined.
subtitle: Grace held back what their words had earned
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is addressed to believers who had joined the talk, like Mistah, Hassan and Hamnah bint Jahsh. Allah {reward}accepted their repentance{/reward} and forgave them because of their faith. He notes the hypocrites behind the lie are {trap}not the ones meant here.{/trap}
now: You were part of a conversation once that tore someone down. You laughed, or added a line. Nothing happened to you. This verse says why: {reward}not because it was fine, but because Allah was merciful.{/reward} That mercy is an invitation to turn back, not a pass.
old: Nothing bad came of it, so it must not have been that serious.
new: If I was spared, it was Allah's mercy, and mercy calls me to repent.
try: Think of one time you joined in mocking or gossip. Ask Allah's forgiveness for it by name.

title: You thought it was small. With Allah it was huge.
subtitle: How a rumor moves from tongue to tongue
then: Mujahid and Sa'id bin Jubayr described it: {trap}I heard this from so-and-so, and so-and-so said such and such.{/trap} People passed it along without knowing anything. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that a person may say a word that angers Allah {trap}without paying any attention to it.{/trap}
now: Voice notes. Screenshots. "Don't tell anyone, but..." You pass it on in ten seconds while waiting for the kettle. It feels like nothing. This verse sets two scales side by side: {idea}what feels small on your tongue can be huge with Allah.{/idea}
old: It was just a few words in passing.
new: A few words about someone's honor can weigh more with Allah than I imagine.
try: Today, notice the moment you are about to repeat something you heard. Pause and let it go.

title: It is not for us to speak of this.
subtitle: The sentence a believer keeps ready
then: Ibn Kathir calls this a further lesson after thinking well of people. If a bad thought about good people is put into the mind by Shaytan, {idea}do not speak about it.{/idea} He cites the hadith that Allah excuses what crosses the mind {reward}as long as it is not spoken or acted on.{/reward}
now: Your cousin starts: "I'm not saying it's true, but..." Everyone leans in. You do not need a speech. Just one line: {idea}"This is not ours to talk about."{/idea} The thought that crossed your mind is not held against you. Saying it would be.
old: If the thought came to me, I might as well say it.
new: A passing thought is excused; letting it out is where I become responsible.
try: Memorize one short line to stop gossip, like this is not ours to talk about, and use it once.

title: Never again, if you truly believe.
subtitle: A warning given like a parent's counsel
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is {idea}forbidding and warning them against anything like this again{/idea} in the future. The words if you are believers tie it to faith in Allah, His laws, and {reward}respect for His Messenger ﷺ.{/reward}
now: You promised yourself after the last family fight that you would never bring up her past again. Then the next argument comes, and it is right there. This verse is Allah saying: {idea}never again, ever.{/idea} Not as a threat. As a promise worth keeping because you believe.
old: I slipped once; it will probably happen again.
new: Allah warns me lovingly so I can make never again part of my faith.
try: Pick one hurtful thing you tend to repeat about someone. Decide today you will not say it again.

title: He spells it out because He knows us.
subtitle: Clear verses from the Knowing, the Wise

picture.label: What Allah gives after the trial

row.title: too many rules
sub: just let us figure it out

then: After a month of confusion and pain, Allah made matters plain. Ibn Kathir explains {idea}He makes clear His rulings and decrees,{/idea} and He knows {reward}what is right for His servants{/reward} and is Wise in what He lays down.
now: When a family crisis hits, everyone has an opinion. Your aunt says one thing, a video says another, your own heart says a third. In the middle of that noise, {idea}clear guidance is a gift.{/idea} It comes from the One who actually knows you.
old: Clear rules feel like they limit me.
new: Clarity from the All-Knowing is care for me, not a cage.
try: When you face a confusing choice this week, look for what Allah has made clear about it first.

title: Even enjoying the spread of indecency is a sin.
subtitle: The heart that likes to see others exposed

picture.label: What the verse looks inside for

row.title: even loving to hear it
sub: the heart is part of it

then: Ibn Kathir calls this a third lesson for those who hear evil talk, half believe it, and start to spread it. He cites the hadith: {trap}do not seek out people's hidden faults,{/trap} for whoever does so, {trap}Allah will expose his faults{/trap} even inside his own house.
now: Someone you dislike gets caught in a scandal. You refresh the thread again and again. A small part of you is glad. This verse names that feeling. {idea}Allah knows what you do not,{/idea} including the full story you are enjoying half of.
old: I am not spreading it, I am just following along.
new: Even enjoying someone's exposure is something Allah sees and weighs.
try: Close one thread, page or chat today that feeds you other people's scandals.

title: Grace again, because Allah is Kind.
subtitle: The third reminder of mercy in this story
then: Once again in this passage Allah says: had it not been for His grace and mercy. Ibn Kathir explains that otherwise {trap}it would have been another matter altogether.{/trap} But He is full of kindness and {reward}accepts the repentance of those who turn to Him.{/reward}
now: You have read through the whole slander story and recognized yourself in parts of it. The forwarded message. The half-belief. The thrill of the gossip. This verse lands right there: {reward}Allah is Kind.{/reward} The point was never to crush you. It was to bring you back.
old: After what I have said about people, I am past mercy.
new: Allah keeps reminding me of His kindness so I will turn back, not give up.
try: Say Ya Ra'uf, Ya Rahim three times today and ask for help with your tongue.

title: Shaytan never asks for the whole thing. Only a step.
subtitle: Footsteps, and the grace that purifies

row.title: Allah purifies
sub: without Him, not one of us

then: Coming right after the slander, this verse names how it spread: {trap}step by step.{/trap} Qatadah said every sin is one of Shaytan's footsteps. Ibn Kathir explains that without Allah's grace {reward}no one would ever be purified,{/reward} since He is the one who helps people turn back.
now: It never starts with the scandal. It starts with opening the app "just to check." Then one comment. Then one reply you would not say to their face. {trap}Each step feels small.{/trap} The verse asks you to notice the first one, and to ask Allah for the purity you cannot make alone.
old: I would never do something that bad.
new: Big wrongs are small steps added up, and only Allah's grace keeps me pure.
try: Name one small first step that usually leads you somewhere you regret. Skip it once today.

title: Would you not love Allah to forgive you?
subtitle: Abu Bakr, Mistah, and the oath he took back

row.title: an oath
sub: I will never spend on him

then: Mistah was Abu Bakr's poor cousin, an emigrant who lived on what Abu Bakr spent on him. After Mistah joined the slander against Aishah, Abu Bakr swore never to help him again. When this verse came, he said, {reward}of course we love that You forgive us,{/reward} and {idea}resumed his spending forever.{/idea}
now: Your brother said something unforgivable about your spouse at a wedding. You cut him off. Now he is short on rent and calls you. This verse does not erase what he did. It asks you a question: {reward}would you not love Allah to forgive you?{/reward}
old: After what they did, I owe them nothing.
new: When I pardon those who wronged me, I am asking Allah to pardon me.
try: Think of one relative you have closed a door on. Send them one kind word, or one small help.

title: Slandering the innocent and unaware is a grave sin.
subtitle: Women who never even thought of what they were accused of
then: Ibn Kathir notes this was revealed because of Aishah, and the Mothers of the believers are first in it. He cites the hadith listing seven destructive sins, among them {trap}accusing chaste, unaware believing women.{/trap} Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd said it applies {idea}to anyone who does the same to Muslim women.{/idea}
now: She is the quiet girl at university. Someone invents a story about her and it spreads through three group chats. She has no idea. She just notices people staring. This verse stands with her. {idea}Her unawareness is part of her innocence,{/idea} and the weight falls on those talking.
old: If she did nothing, the gossip cannot really hurt her.
new: Allah counts slandering an innocent, unaware person among the most destructive sins.
try: If you know someone being talked about unfairly, quietly defend them once in the next conversation.

title: Your own tongue, hands and feet will testify.
subtitle: The witnesses you carry everywhere
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ described a servant who argues with his Lord, refusing any witness but himself. Allah says, {idea}you are enough as a witness against yourself.{/idea} His mouth is sealed and {trap}his limbs speak of his deeds.{/trap}
now: The thumb that typed it. The feet that walked into that room. The tongue that said "I swear I didn't." You carry your witnesses everywhere. {idea}They are listening now.{/idea} That is not a reason for fear alone. It is a reason to give them better things to say.
old: If I deny it well enough, it is as if it did not happen.
new: My own body keeps the record and will speak it plainly.
try: Tonight, look at your hands and ask: what did they do today that I would want them to tell?

title: That Day, everyone will see that Allah is the Truth.
subtitle: The account paid in full, with no unfairness
then: Ibn Abbas said the word here means {idea}their account.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains that on that Day people will know Allah's promise, His threat and His reckoning are {idea}all just, with no unfairness in them.{/idea}
now: The colleague who lied about you got promoted. The cousin who spread the story never apologized. It feels like they won. This verse is the long view: {idea}every account is paid in full.{/idea} You do not have to settle it yourself. You only have to make sure your own account is clean.
old: They got away with it.
new: No one gets away with anything; the Truth settles every account in full.
try: Hand one unresolved wrong done to you over to Allah in a short dua, and stop replaying it today.

title: Evil words suit evil people. Aishah was free of them.
subtitle: What the slander says about those who spoke it
then: Ibn Abbas said this was revealed about Aishah and the people of the slander. Ibn Jarir explained that {trap}evil speech is more suited to evil people.{/trap} What the hypocrites said fit them, not her. Ibn Kathir adds it implies a promise that she will be {reward}the Prophet's ﷺ wife in Paradise.{/reward}
now: When someone tells you something ugly about another person, notice what it reveals. Often it says more about the speaker than the subject. {idea}Words carry the scent of where they come from.{/idea} And the words you choose about others say who you are.
old: When someone is accused of something ugly, it says something about them.
new: Ugly words usually describe the one who says them; good people are kept clear of them.
try: Listen to your own words about others for one day. Ask what they say about you.

title: A home is a private world. Knock and greet first.
subtitle: Asking permission puts people at ease

row.title: a formality
sub: we are close, just walk in

row.title: their ease
sub: Ibn Abbas: putting people at ease

then: Muqatil said that before Islam people walked straight into each other's homes, which was hard on those inside. Ibn Kathir reports that Jabir knocked and answered {trap}it is me{/trap} and the Prophet ﷺ disliked it. Abdullah bin Mas'ud would {idea}clear his throat at his own door{/idea} so his family was not startled.
now: Your teenager's bedroom. Your parents' room. A friend's flat where you have a key. A colleague's office door left half open. The verse is about all of them in spirit: {idea}people deserve a moment to be ready for you.{/idea} A knock and a salaam is a small kindness.
old: We are family, so I can just walk in.
new: Asking first is a way of honoring the people inside, even the closest ones.
try: Knock and say salaam before entering one room at home today, even if the door is open.

title: If they say go back, go back. It is purer.
subtitle: Hearing no without taking offense
then: Ibn Kathir reports that Abu Musa asked permission three times at Umar's door and, with no answer, {idea}simply left.{/idea} He cited the Prophet's ﷺ words that if permission is not given after three times, one should go away. Umar later asked for a witness, and the youngest of the Ansar confirmed it.
now: You show up at a friend's place unannounced. They say through the intercom, "Now is not a good time." Your face gets hot. This verse cools it: {reward}going back is purer for you.{/reward} Their no is not an attack. It is their right, and accepting it is your good deed.
old: If they turn me away, they must not care about me.
new: Turning back gracefully when told no is purer, and Allah sees it.
try: The next time someone says not now, reply with a warm okay and no follow-up guilt.

title: Allah knows what you show and what you hide.
subtitle: Ease in public spaces, with the heart still watched
then: After the manners of entering homes, Allah eases things for places where no one lives and people have a need. The verse closes by reminding them that {idea}Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.{/idea}
now: The shared office kitchen. The station waiting room. The empty hall at the mosque. No permission needed. But you still know why you walked in. {idea}The ease is real, and so is the One who sees your reason.{/idea}
old: If no one owns the space, nothing I do there matters.
new: Open spaces are an ease from Allah, and my hidden intentions still count.
try: In a shared space today, leave it a little better than you found it.

title: Guarding the eyes is how you guard the heart.
subtitle: The first glance, and what to do with the second
then: Ibn Kathir explains that since looking provokes the heart, the verse joins guarding the gaze with guarding chastity. Jarir asked the Prophet ﷺ about the sudden glance, and he told him {idea}to turn his eyes away.{/idea} An early saying adds that whoever guards his gaze, {reward}Allah illuminates his heart.{/reward}
now: Your feed autoplays something you did not choose. A billboard on the commute. A colleague's photos. The first glance just happens. {idea}The second is a choice.{/idea} Scroll past, look up, look away. Each time is a small gift to your own heart.
old: Looking is not doing anything.
new: What I let my eyes rest on shapes my heart, so guarding them is purity.
try: Today, every time your eyes land on something you would not want in your heart, look away within a second.

title: Turn to Allah, all of you, that you may succeed.
subtitle: Modesty for believing women, and a call to everyone

picture.label: What the verse asks of believing women

key.label: How the first women heard it

then: Ibn Kathir notes this distinguished the believing women from the customs of the Jahiliyyah. Aishah said, {reward}may Allah have mercy on the women of the early emigrants:{/reward} when this verse came, they tore their wraps to cover themselves. The verse ends by turning to everyone: {idea}repent to Allah, all of you.{/idea}
now: Everyone has a part of their faith they keep meaning to get to. A habit, a choice of clothes, a way of speaking, a screen they should close. The early emigrant women responded the same day. And the verse does not end with one group. {idea}It ends with all of you, turning back together.{/idea}
old: This verse is about other people's choices.
new: Every believer is called to turn back to Allah, and success lies in that turning.
try: Pick one thing you have been meaning to change for Allah's sake. Take the first step today.

title: Poverty is not the end of the conversation.
subtitle: Helping the single to marry, and Allah's promise to enrich

key.label: What decides if it is time

then: Ibn Kathir explains the word for the single covers men and women, never married or widowed or divorced. Ibn Mas'ud said, {reward}seek richness through marriage.{/reward} He also tells of a man who owned only his waist wrap, and the Prophet ﷺ married him with the promise to {idea}teach his bride the Qur'an he knew.{/idea}
now: Your friend is ready, the match is good, but everyone keeps saying: wait till you own a flat, a car, a big wedding budget. Years pass. This verse speaks to the whole community, not just the couple: {idea}help them,{/idea} and trust that {reward}Allah enriches from His bounty.{/reward}
old: We cannot think about marriage until the money is sorted.
new: Allah promises to enrich those who seek chastity, and the community is asked to help.
try: If someone you know is trying to marry, offer one practical help: an introduction, advice, or a small gift.

title: Waiting with dignity, and freeing others from their chains.
subtitle: Chastity while waiting, and mercy for the forced
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that Allah has taken it upon Himself to help {reward}one who marries seeking chastity and one working to buy his freedom.{/reward} Ikrimah advised one who could not marry to {idea}ponder the heavens and the earth{/idea} until Allah gave him means. The verse also condemns forcing anyone into indecency for worldly gain.
now: You are 29, the right person has not come, or the money is not there yet. Everyone else's wedding photos keep coming. This verse sees you: {idea}keep your dignity while you wait,{/idea} Allah will open a way. And if you have more, it reminds you that it is {reward}Allah's wealth{/reward} that can help someone else get free.
old: Waiting this long means something is wrong with me.
new: Waiting with chastity is honored by Allah, and His help is promised.
try: If you are waiting for something you cannot have yet, spend ten minutes today outside, looking at the sky, like Ikrimah advised.

title: Clear verses, old stories, and a word for the mindful.
subtitle: Three things Allah sent down so far in this surah
then: Ibn Kathir notes these verses contain {idea}clear rulings and firm commands.{/idea} After the slander, the limits, the manners of the home, and marriage, Allah pauses: He has sent plain verses, examples from earlier peoples, and {reward}an admonition for those who are mindful of Him.{/reward}
now: You have read twenty or thirty verses and some of it hit close. The rumor you passed on. The door you walked through without knocking. This verse is a pause button. {idea}What did you just learn?{/idea} The same words wash over some people and change others.
old: I have read it, so I have got it.
new: Clear verses become admonition only when I let them change me.
try: Write down one line from this surah so far that changed how you think. Keep it on your phone's lock screen.

title: Light upon light: the Quran meeting a ready heart.
subtitle: The parable of the niche, the lamp and the glass
then: Ibn Abbas said Allah is the Light of the heavens and earth means {idea}their Guide.{/idea} Ubayy bin Ka'b said the glass is the believer's heart, the lamp is the Qur'an and faith. As-Suddi said the fire and oil {reward}only give light together,{/reward} like the Qur'an and faith. The Prophet ﷺ used to praise Allah as this Light in his night prayer.
now: You know the feeling: a verse you heard a hundred times suddenly lands on you in a hard week. The verse did not change. Your heart was {idea}clean enough, ready enough, to catch it.{/idea} Keep the glass clear, and the light that comes is {reward}light upon light.{/reward}
old: I either feel spiritual or I do not; it is just my mood.
new: Light comes from Allah; my part is a clear heart and a lamp of Quran inside it.
try: Read this verse slowly once today, then ask Allah: put light in my heart.

title: The lamp has a home: houses raised for His name.
subtitle: Why the masjid follows the parable of light

row.title: remembrance
sub: built for what it was built for

then: Ibn Kathir explains that after likening the heart to a lamp, Allah names {idea}where it belongs: the masjids,{/idea} the places most beloved to Him. Ibn Abbas said idle talk was forbidden in them. A man once called out in the masjid about a lost camel, and the Prophet ﷺ said {trap}the masjids were built only for what they were built for.{/trap}
now: You walk into the masjid and your phone is already out. A bit of business chat by the shoe rack. Then the iqamah. This verse makes the masjid {reward}a place where the lamp gets refilled.{/reward} Leave the rest at the door, even for ten minutes.
old: The masjid is where I go to pray quickly and leave.
new: The masjid is the home Allah raised for the light in my heart.
try: Next time you enter a masjid, say the dua: O Allah, open the gates of Your mercy for me. Then put your phone away.

title: Busy people whose business never pulls them away.
subtitle: Traders who still keep their prayer
then: Right after describing the houses where Allah is remembered, the verse describes the people who fill them. They are traders and workers, yet {idea}neither trade nor sale distracts them{/idea} from remembering Allah, prayer, and zakah. What drives them is {trap}fear of a Day when hearts and eyes turn about.{/trap}
now: Payday. Quarter end. A client call running into Asr. You are not asked to quit your job. The verse praises people who {idea}have a busy job and still stop for prayer.{/idea} The deal can wait ten minutes. Your heart is the one thing that cannot be outsourced.
old: I am too busy at work to pray on time.
new: Allah praises people who are busy in trade but never distracted from Him.
try: Set a reminder for one prayer at work today and stop on time, even mid-task.

title: Rewarded for their best, then more, without counting.
subtitle: What those faithful traders receive
then: The verse completes the picture of those who keep prayer through trade. Allah will reward them {reward}according to the best of what they did{/reward} and then add more from His bounty. The verse ends by saying Allah provides {reward}without account{/reward} to whom He wills.
now: At work, you get paid for hours logged. Bonuses are rare, and audited. This verse describes a different employer. He looks at {reward}your best moment{/reward} and pays by that, then gives more on top, and does not count it out coin by coin.
old: My good deeds will be measured exactly, the bad against the good.
new: Allah rewards by my best deeds and then adds more without measure.
try: Do one good deed today with full effort, as if it were the one you will be rewarded by.

title: A mirage looks like water until you reach it.
subtitle: Deeds that look full from far away
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is a parable of those who think they have good deeds and beliefs, but when Allah examines them, {trap}nothing is accepted,{/trap} because faith or sincerity was missing. Like a thirsty man who reaches the shimmer, he finds nothing, but {idea}finds Allah there,{/idea} who settles his account.
now: The charity post with your name on it. The volunteering for the photo. The long prayer when people are watching. From far away it looks like water. This verse asks you to check your own deeds now, {idea}while there is still time to make them real.{/idea}
old: I have done so many good things, I must be fine.
new: A deed without faith and sincerity is a mirage; I want my deeds to be real water.
try: Pick one good deed you do mostly to be seen. Do it once this week where no one will know.

title: Darkness on darkness, and only Allah gives light.
subtitle: Following the crowd without knowing where it goes
then: Ibn Kathir says this second parable is for one who simply follows, not knowing who he follows or where. Like the man asked where he was going: {trap}with them. And where are they going? I do not know.{/trap} He contrasts it with Allah guiding to His light whom He wills, and ends: {reward}we ask Allah to increase us in light.{/reward}
now: Everyone at work is doing it. Everyone in the family group thinks that way. Everyone online is saying this. If someone asked you why, you would say: because they are. This verse is about {idea}checking where the crowd is actually going,{/idea} and asking Allah for light of your own.
old: If everyone around me is doing it, it is probably fine.
new: Following without knowing is darkness; light is something I ask Allah for.
try: Make the dua today: O Allah, put light in my heart, light on my right and on my left.

title: Even the birds in flight know how to praise Him.
subtitle: Every creature has its own prayer

row.title: its own prayer
sub: the way it was guided to

then: Ibn Kathir explains that angels, humans, jinn, animals and even inanimate things glorify Allah. The birds glorify Him {idea}while they are flying,{/idea} each with the way it was inspired and guided to. He compares it to the verse that the seven heavens and earth glorify Him.
now: You are stuck in traffic, scrolling. Above the windscreen a flock of birds turns in the sky. They are not wasting the moment. {idea}They are in prayer, in their own way.{/idea} You are the one creature who can choose whether to join.
old: Nature is just scenery while I get on with life.
new: Everything around me is already praising Allah; I am invited to join.
try: The next time you see birds flying, say SubhanAllah once with them.

title: Everything belongs to Him, and everything returns to Him.
subtitle: The owner and the destination are the same
then: After showing all creation praising Allah, the verse names Him the owner of all. Ibn Kathir explains He is {idea}the Ruler and Controller,{/idea} and the return to Him is on the Day of Resurrection, when He will judge. He closes with {reward}to Him be praise at the beginning and in the end.{/reward}
now: The mortgage papers say it is yours. The payslip says the salary is yours. The verse reads both documents and adds a line: {idea}borrowed, and returning.{/idea} It is not a threat. It is relief. You are not holding the whole world up. He is.
old: I need to control everything I own.
new: Everything belongs to Allah and returns to Him, including me.
try: Look at one thing you worry about owning or losing. Say: it belongs to Allah, and to Him it returns.

title: Watch a storm form and see Whose hand is in it.
subtitle: Clouds driven, joined, piled, and opened
then: Ibn Kathir describes Allah driving the clouds from when they are {idea}still weak,{/idea} then joining and piling them, and rain coming from the gaps. Ubayd bin Umayr spoke of winds that stir, form, join and seed the clouds. The rain and hail may be {reward}mercy for some{/reward} and held back from others.
now: The weather app shows a storm coming. You check it to see if your commute will be wet. Next time, step outside and watch it build. {idea}Every step was driven.{/idea} The flash that makes you squint is a reminder of how small your eyes are next to His power.
old: Weather is just the climate doing its thing.
new: Every cloud is driven, joined, and opened by Allah, as mercy or as warning.
try: The next time it rains, step to a window and make a dua while it falls.

title: Night and day trade places, and it is a lesson.
subtitle: Something lengthens, something shortens, by His command
then: Ibn Kathir explains Allah {idea}takes from the length of one and adds to the other{/idea} until they are equal, then reverses it. He controls this by His command, power and knowledge. He links it to the verse that the alternation of night and day holds {reward}signs for people of understanding.{/reward}
now: Your alarm goes off in the dark in winter. In summer it is already light. You complain both times. The verse asks you to {idea}look up from the complaint.{/idea} The same hand that shifts the seasons shifts the hard and easy seasons of your life.
old: Days just go by.
new: Every turning of night into day is a sign for those who look.
try: Watch the sunset or sunrise once this week without your phone, and just notice it.

title: One water, and a world of creatures from it.
subtitle: Bellies, two legs, four legs, as He wills

row.title: He creates what He wills
sub: He is able to do all

then: Ibn Kathir notes Allah mentions His power to create all kinds of animals, {idea}with their different forms, colors and ways of moving,{/idea} from one kind of water. What He wills happens, and {reward}He is able to do all things.{/reward}
now: Your toddler is fascinated by an ant on the pavement. A dog walks past. A pigeon lands. You are rushing to the car. The verse slows you down: {idea}all of it came from water,{/idea} each made differently on purpose. Your child is seeing something true.
old: Animals are just background to my day.
new: Every creature, so different, is a sign of the One who creates what He wills.
try: Stop for one minute today and really look at an animal. Notice how it moves.

title: The verses are clear. Guidance is His to give.
subtitle: A short line between the signs and the hypocrites
then: After the signs of clouds, night and day and animals, the verse sums up. Ibn Kathir explains Allah has sent {idea}clear rulings, words of wisdom and parables,{/idea} and guides people of understanding to {reward}ponder and understand them.{/reward}
now: You have watched a dozen videos on faith and still feel unsure. It is not more information you need. {idea}The verses are already clear.{/idea} What you ask for is guidance itself, and that is asked of Allah, not of the algorithm.
old: I need one more proof before I commit.
new: The signs are clear; guidance is a gift I ask Allah for.
try: In your next prayer, say Ihdina as-sirat al-mustaqim slowly and mean it as a request.

title: We believe and we obey, said the ones who turned away.
subtitle: When the words and the actions part ways
then: Ibn Kathir describes the hypocrites of Madinah, {trap}who show one thing while hiding another.{/trap} They said they believed and obeyed, then turned away. Their actions contradicted their words: {trap}they say what they do not do.{/trap}
now: You say yes in the family meeting, then quietly do the opposite. You agree in the team call, then never follow through. Small versions of this live in all of us. The verse is a mirror, {idea}not a label for someone else.{/idea}
old: I said the right thing, so I am on the right side.
new: Faith is proven when my actions keep the promise my words made.
try: Find one promise you made to Allah or to someone and did not keep. Keep it today.

title: Called to judgment, they turned aside.
subtitle: Refusing the standard when it might go against you
then: Ibn Kathir explains that when the hypocrites were asked to follow the guidance revealed to the Messenger ﷺ, {trap}they turned away, too proud of themselves.{/trap} He compares it to the verses about those who claim belief but turn away from the Prophet ﷺ with aversion.
now: A family inheritance. A business split. You know what is fair according to your faith. You also know a cleverer route that gives you more. {trap}The moment you look away from the standard{/trap} is the moment this verse describes. It is a test of the heart, not of the lawyer.
old: I will follow the guidance when it is convenient.
new: Turning from Allah's standard when it costs me shows what my heart really holds.
try: Think of one disagreement you are in. Ask honestly: what would be fair before Allah?

title: When the ruling suited them, they came running.
subtitle: Obedience that depends on winning
then: Ibn Kathir explains that if the judgment was going to be in their favor, they came and listened and obeyed. But {trap}their acceptance was not because it was the truth,{/trap} only because it matched their desires. When the truth went against them, {trap}they turned away from it.{/trap}
now: You quote the hadith about rights of the husband, or the wife, or the parents, when it helps your side. The ones that ask something of you, you skip. Everyone does it a little. The verse asks: {idea}do I follow the truth, or does the truth follow me?{/idea}
old: I follow the religion when it backs me up.
new: Following the truth only when it favors me is following my desire.
try: Find one teaching you tend to quote against others. Apply it to yourself today.

title: Disease, doubt, or fear of unfairness? None of these.
subtitle: Three questions about a turning heart
then: Ibn Kathir explains the verse's questions: either their hearts had a disease, or they doubted the religion, or they feared Allah and His Messenger ﷺ would wrong them. Allah answers: {trap}it is they who are the wrongdoers.{/trap} Allah and His Messenger ﷺ {idea}are free of the unfairness they imagine.{/idea}
now: When you resist something Allah asks, notice the story you tell yourself. "It is unfair to me." "It does not fit modern life." "Maybe it is not really from Allah." The verse invites you to check {idea}the heart that is telling the story.{/idea}
old: When I resist a teaching, the teaching must be the problem.
new: Resistance to what Allah asks often comes from a disease, doubt, or fear in me.
try: Ask Allah tonight to heal your heart from any doubt or disease it is carrying.

title: Two words that settle a dispute: we hear, we obey.
subtitle: The believer's answer when called to Allah's judgment
then: After the hypocrites who turned away, Allah describes the believers' only answer. Ibn Kathir reports that Ubadah bin As-Samit, a veteran of Badr, told his nephew on his deathbed: {idea}listen and obey when times are easy and hard,{/idea} when you feel energetic and when you do not, and {idea}train your tongue to speak the truth.{/idea}
now: Fajr alarm in winter. A family argument where you know what is fair but it costs you. A habit you know you should drop. The answer in this verse is not a feeling. It is a choice you say out loud: {reward}we hear, and we obey,{/reward} even on the days you do not want to.
old: I will follow when I feel ready and it makes sense to me.
new: Success is saying we hear and we obey, in the easy times and the hard ones.
try: Pick one thing you know Allah asks of you and have been putting off. Do it today, even half-heartedly.

title: Obey, fear the past, guard the future: that is winning.
subtitle: Three parts of the people who truly attain

row.title: all goodness
sub: in this world and the next

then: Ibn Kathir explains each part: obeying in what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden, {idea}fearing Allah for past sins,{/idea} and {idea}having taqwa about sins one might commit in the future.{/idea} Such people will {reward}attain all goodness and be saved from all evil{/reward} in both worlds.
now: Your past has things you regret. Your future has temptations you can already see coming. Today sits in between. This verse gives one shape for all three: {idea}obey now, feel the weight of yesterday, guard tomorrow.{/idea} That is what winning looks like.
old: Success is getting what I want in life.
new: Success is obeying now, fearing Allah for the past, and guarding the future.
try: Name one past sin to ask forgiveness for, and one future situation to guard against. Do both today.

title: Do not swear. Your obedience is already known.
subtitle: Big oaths standing in for small actions
then: Ibn Kathir explains the hypocrites swore that if the Prophet ﷺ ordered them out, they would go. The reply: do not swear, {trap}your obedience is known,{/trap} meaning it is only verbal and not followed by action. He links it to verses where they {trap}use their oaths as a screen.{/trap}
now: "Next month I will start, I promise." "Wallahi this time is different." You hear yourself swearing bigger the more you have failed before. The verse cuts through: {idea}no need to swear.{/idea} Allah is acquainted with what you do. Let the doing speak.
old: If I promise strongly enough, it shows I am serious.
new: Allah knows what I do; a quiet action is worth more than a loud oath.
try: Instead of promising to start something, do five minutes of it today without telling anyone.

title: He carries his duty. You carry yours.
subtitle: The Messenger conveys clearly; the response is ours
then: Ibn Kathir explains the Messenger ﷺ is responsible for {idea}conveying the message and fulfilling the trust,{/idea} and the people for accepting it and doing as it commands. He links it to the verses: your duty is only to convey, and {idea}you are not a dictator over them.{/idea}
now: You keep waiting for someone to make you pray, make you change, make you believe more firmly. The message has already reached you, clearly. {idea}Your part is the response.{/idea} And if you are the parent or friend trying to convey it, your part is to convey well, not to force.
old: If I am not living my faith, it is because no one pushed me.
new: The message was conveyed clearly; my response is my own responsibility.
try: If you are trying to guide someone, share one thing kindly today and leave the rest to Allah.

title: After their fear, He promised security.
subtitle: A promise to believers who worship Him alone
then: Abu Al-Aliyah said the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions lived in fear in Makkah, and in Madinah they {trap}carried their weapons morning and evening.{/trap} Al-Bara said this verse came {trap}in a time of extreme fear.{/trap} Allah later gave them safety. Abu Al-Aliyah added: {idea}they changed, so their situation changed.{/idea}
now: You are afraid. Of the job going, the diagnosis, the rent, a family falling apart. The verse is addressed to people who had real fear. Its promise is tied to one thing you can control: {idea}worshipping Allah without partners, with good deeds.{/idea} The rest is His promise to keep.
old: My security depends on my circumstances.
new: Allah promises security after fear to those who worship Him alone.
try: Name one fear you are carrying. Pray two rakahs today and hand it to Allah by name.

title: Prayer, zakah, obedience: the road to mercy.
subtitle: Worship of Allah and kindness to His creatures
then: Right after the promise of security, the verse names the daily practice behind it. Ibn Kathir explains prayer is {idea}worshipping Allah alone,{/idea} zakah is {reward}kindness towards His poor and weak creatures,{/reward} and by these one obeys the Messenger ﷺ, so that Allah will have mercy.
now: You pray on the way to work, give a little on payday, and try to follow the Sunnah in small things. It does not feel like much. This verse says {reward}that is the road to mercy.{/reward} One line upward to Allah, one line outward to people.
old: Mercy is something that will just happen to me.
new: Prayer, giving, and following the Messenger ﷺ are how I walk toward Allah's mercy.
try: Give a small amount to someone in need today, right after a prayer.

title: No one outruns Allah anywhere on earth.
subtitle: A word of comfort to the Prophet ﷺ
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}do not think{/idea} those who opposed and denied you can flee from Allah. He is able to deal with them, and their end in the Hereafter is {trap}a wretched destination.{/trap}
now: Sometimes it looks like people who do wrong just keep going. No consequences. Bigger house every year. This verse is not for gloating. It is for {idea}steadying your own heart:{/idea} no one is outside Allah's reach. So you can stop measuring and keep your own path straight.
old: Wrongdoers seem to get away with everything.
new: No one escapes Allah, so I can let go and keep my own path straight.
try: When you feel bitter about someone getting away with wrong, say hasbiyAllah and turn to your own task.

title: Even inside your home, some hours are private.
subtitle: Three times of rest, and teaching children to knock
then: Earlier the surah taught how strangers ask to enter. Ibn Kathir notes these verses turn to {idea}those who live in the same house,{/idea} like young children and servants. Outside the three times, they move about freely, since they {reward}go around the house serving and helping.{/reward} Ibn Abbas lamented that {trap}most people had stopped following it.{/trap}
now: Your six-year-old bursts into your room at 6am, every day. You laugh, but you also wish they knocked. This verse gives the family {idea}a gentle shared rhythm:{/idea} three times when even little ones ask first. It is not coldness. It is teaching respect at home.
old: Little children do not need to learn privacy yet.
new: Allah teaches even young children to respect the private hours of a home.
try: Teach a child at home, kindly, to knock and wait at your door at one of these three times.

title: When children grow up, their manners grow up too.
subtitle: Reaching maturity means asking like the adults do
then: Ibn Kathir explains that once children who used to ask at the three times reach puberty, {idea}they ask permission as the adults before them did,{/idea} not only at those times. Allah ends again: this is how He makes the verses clear, and He is {reward}Knowing and Wise.{/reward}
now: Your son is suddenly taller than you. He wants his own room, his own rules, his own phone password. This verse adds the other half of growing up: {idea}he knocks, too.{/idea} Respect for privacy flows both ways once a child becomes an adult.
old: Growing up means getting more rights.
new: Growing up means taking on the manners of adults, including asking first.
try: If you have a teenager, talk with them today about knocking and privacy, both ways.

title: An ease is given, and restraint is still called better.
subtitle: Older women, ease, and the choice of modesty
then: Ibn Kathir notes this speaks of women past childbearing who no longer seek marriage. Allah eases things for them, without any {trap}display of adornment.{/trap} Then He adds that {idea}to refrain is better for them,{/idea} even though the ease is there. The verse closes: Allah is Hearing and Knowing.
now: Your grandmother could choose the easier option and nobody would blame her. She still holds to the extra step, quietly, because she loves it. This verse honors that: {idea}between allowed and better is a space for love.{/idea} Many good deeds live in that space.
old: If something is allowed, there is no reason to do more.
new: Allah gives ease and still points to what is better, leaving room for love.
try: Choose one thing today where you could take the easy way, and take the better one instead, just for Allah.

title: Eat together, eat with the disabled, and greet as you enter.
subtitle: Removing awkwardness from shared meals
then: Sa'id bin Jubayr said people felt awkward eating with the blind, lame or sick, {trap}fearing they might be unfair to them.{/trap} Ad-Dahhak said some were too proud. Mujahid said the disabled felt ashamed being taken to others' homes. Allah removed it all. A man told the Prophet ﷺ they ate but felt unsatisfied, and he said: {reward}eat together and mention Allah's name.{/reward}
now: Your uncle in a wheelchair always ends up eating in another room "so he is comfortable." The friend who lives alone eats standing at the counter. This verse pulls the chairs back to the table. {reward}Eat together.{/reward} And when you walk into your own home tonight, say salaam, even if the house is empty.
old: It is easier for everyone if some people eat separately.
new: Allah removes the awkwardness; blessing is in eating together and greeting with peace.
try: Invite someone who usually eats alone to share a meal with you this week. Say salaam when you enter.

title: True believers ask before they leave.
subtitle: Manners for leaving a shared gathering
then: Ibn Kathir explains that just as Allah taught them to ask permission to enter, He taught them to {idea}ask permission to leave{/idea} when gathered with the Prophet ﷺ for something shared, like Friday prayer or a consultation. He cites the hadith: give salaam when you join a gathering and when you leave, {idea}the first is not more important than the last.{/idea}
now: The community meeting is running long. You have somewhere to be. You could just quietly vanish. Or you could catch the organizer's eye, say "I need to head off, salaam." This verse makes that small moment {idea}a sign of real faith,{/idea} and a reason for prayers on your behalf.
old: Leaving early quietly is more polite than interrupting.
new: Asking and greeting when I leave a shared matter is part of real faith.
try: The next time you leave a gathering, say salaam on your way out.

title: He is holding you back from the fire. Do not slip away.
subtitle: Honoring the Messenger ﷺ and his way
then: Ibn Abbas said people used to call him O Muhammad, and Allah taught them to say {idea}O Messenger of Allah.{/idea} Muqatil said some hypocrites would {trap}hide behind others and sneak out{/trap} during the Friday sermon. Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ parable: {reward}I am holding you by your waist, away from the fire,{/reward} and you overwhelm me and rush in.
now: Moths circle a streetlight at night and keep throwing themselves at it. You watch from your balcony and wonder why. Then you think of the habits you keep flying back to, after being warned. {reward}Someone is still holding your waist.{/reward} The Sunnah is his hand. Do not slip out of it.
old: The Sunnah is a set of nice extras.
new: The Prophet's ﷺ way is a hand pulling me back from harm.
try: Pick one Sunnah you have dropped and bring it back today, with love for the one who taught it.

title: He already knows where you stand.
subtitle: The surah closes with Allah's knowledge of everything
then: Ibn Kathir closes the surah by noting that Allah knows what His servants do {idea}in secret and in the open,{/idea} and not one speck is hidden from Him. On the Day of return, He will inform each person of what they did, {trap}major and minor.{/trap} He compares it to a book that leaves out nothing small or big.
now: A whole surah about rumors, homes, eyes, doors, meals and light. It all ends here: {idea}Allah knows where you stand.{/idea} Not where you say you stand. Not where your feed says. The real place. That is scary only until you remember He also knows every effort you made to turn back.
old: No one really knows what I am going through.
new: Allah knows exactly where I stand, and every step I take toward Him.
try: Tonight, sit for two minutes and tell Allah honestly where you stand. He already knows.
